vocab.meaning: fairly large or important

vocab.meaning: help something to develop

vocab.meaning: existing in large quantities

vocab.meaning: grow and succeed

vocab.meaning: have enough space for; adapt to

vocab.example: Sales plateaued at around 200 units a month.

vocab.meaning: certain to happen; impossible to avoid
vocab.example: Some job losses are inevitable as technology advances.

vocab.meaning: the people who live in a place

vocab.meaning: about; not exactly
vocab.example: Approximately 40 per cent of the visitors were under 25.

vocab.meaning: large in amount or importance
vocab.example: There has been a substantial rise in the number of people working from home.

vocab.meaning: go up and down in an irregular way
vocab.example: House prices fluctuated sharply over the decade.

vocab.meaning: control or limit something harmful
vocab.example: Higher taxes could curb the consumption of sugary drinks.

vocab.meaning: able to recover quickly after difficulty
vocab.example: Resilient communities recover faster after floods.

vocab.meaning: make something less serious or harmful
vocab.example: Governments should act to mitigate the effects of climate change.

vocab.meaning: able to continue without harming the environment or running out
vocab.example: We need more sustainable sources of energy.

vocab.meaning: a part of a whole
vocab.example: A large proportion of students study abroad.

vocab.meaning: prevent someone from having something
vocab.example: Long working hours deprive parents of time with their children.

vocab.meaning: something that exists and can be seen or studied
vocab.example: Remote working is a relatively new phenomenon.

vocab.meaning: weaken something little by little
vocab.example: Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.

vocab.meaning: ordinary and rather boring
vocab.example: Robots could do the mundane tasks in offices.

vocab.meaning: causing harm

vocab.meaning: something that encourages people to act
vocab.example: Tax incentives encourage firms to hire young graduates.

vocab.meaning: easy to harm or hurt

vocab.meaning: something that seems bad at first but turns out well

vocab.meaning: seeming reasonable or likely to be true

vocab.meaning: keep something

vocab.meaning: extremely important

vocab.meaning: happening slowly, a little at a time

vocab.meaning: give money or time for a particular purpose

vocab.meaning: find or meet by chance

vocab.meaning: found in many places or among many people

vocab.meaning: depend on someone or something

vocab.meaning: help to cause something
vocab.example: A poor diet contributes to many health problems.

vocab.word: at the end of the day
vocab.meaning: when everything is considered
vocab.example: At the end of the day, practice matters more than talent.

vocab.meaning: a big difference between things that should be equal

vocab.meaning: so small that it is not important
vocab.example: The cost of the change was negligible.

vocab.meaning: very busy and full of activity
vocab.example: My week at university is usually quite hectic.

vocab.meaning: able to be used in many ways
vocab.example: Bamboo is a versatile building material.

vocab.meaning: relaxed and not easily worried
vocab.example: My brother is very laid-back about exams.

vocab.meaning: common at a particular time or place
vocab.example: Obesity is increasingly prevalent among children.

tips.title: True, False or Not Given
tips.body: False means the text says the opposite. Not Given means the text does not say. Use only the passage, never your own knowledge.

tips.title: Skim first, then scan
tips.body: Do not read every word. Skim the title and the first lines of each paragraph for the structure, then scan for key words from the question.

tips.title: Do not memorise essays
tips.body: Examiners recognise memorised answers, and they can lower your score. Learn useful phrases instead and write about the actual question.

tips.title: Look for synonyms
tips.body: The question rarely uses the exact words of the passage. Find the paraphrase: "increase" in the question may be "rise" in the text.

tips.title: Develop your ideas in Part 3
tips.body: Give your opinion, explain why, add an example, and compare the past and the present or different groups of people.

tips.title: It is fine to ask
tips.body: If you do not understand a question, ask the examiner to repeat it. It does not lower your score.

tips.title: Paraphrase to show range
tips.body: If you cannot remember a word, explain it in other words. Using a range of vocabulary matters more than using rare words.

tips.title: Check your essay
tips.body: Keep two or three minutes at the end to check verb tenses, articles (a, an, the), plurals and spelling.

tips.title: Matching headings
tips.body: Read the first and last sentences of each paragraph. The heading is the main idea of the paragraph, not a detail from it.

tips.title: Plan for five minutes
tips.body: Before you write, choose your position and two main ideas, each with an example. A short plan makes the essay clearer and faster to write.

tips.title: Listen for corrections
tips.body: Speakers often change their minds: "Tuesday, no, sorry, Thursday." The final version is the answer, not the first one you hear.

tips.title: Respect the word limit
tips.body: If the instructions say NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS, a three-word answer scores zero. Check the limit on every question.

tips.title: Find your starting point on a map
tips.body: On a map or plan question, find where you are and the compass points before the recording starts. Then follow the directions step by step.

tips.title: Answer every part of the question
tips.body: If the question asks for causes and solutions, write about both. Missing a part limits your score for task response.

tips.title: Stress the important words
tips.body: Good pronunciation is not an accent. It is clear sounds, stressed key words and a natural pace that is neither rushed nor slow.

tips.title: Use the preview time
tips.body: Before each part starts, read the questions and underline the key words. Decide what kind of answer you need: a number, a name, a place.

tips.title: Do not memorise answers
tips.body: Examiners can tell when an answer is learned by heart. Speak naturally about your own life and ideas.

tips.title: Use linking words with care
tips.body: "However" and "In addition" are useful, but not at the start of every sentence. Make the ideas connect first, then add the link.

tips.title: Task 2 counts double
tips.body: Task 2 carries twice the marks of Task 1. Aim for about 20 minutes on Task 1 and 40 on Task 2.

tips.title: Yes, No or Not Given
tips.body: These questions are about the writer's opinion or claims, not facts. Look for words such as "believes", "argues" and "suggests".

tips.title: Use your minute in Part 2
tips.body: Write key words, not sentences. Cover every point on the card and keep speaking until the examiner stops you after two minutes.

tips.title: Watch your time
tips.body: You have 60 minutes for three passages, about 20 for each. Do not spend more than a minute on one question at first.

tips.title: Never leave an answer blank
tips.body: There is no penalty for a wrong answer. Move on from a hard question, come back if you have time, and guess before you finish.

tips.title: Spelling counts
tips.body: A misspelled answer loses the mark. Both British and American spelling are accepted, but check names, plurals and endings.

tips.title: Plurals and numbers
tips.body: Listen for the final -s. "Book" and "books" are different answers. Write numbers carefully: 13 and 30 sound alike.

tips.title: Fluency before perfection
tips.body: Correct yourself calmly and keep going. Phrases like "Well, let me think" give you a moment without a long silence.

tips.title: One idea per paragraph
tips.body: Start each body paragraph with a topic sentence, explain it, then give an example. Do not mix two ideas in one paragraph.

tips.title: Beware of distractors
tips.body: The speaker may mention every option. Listen for the one that is not rejected, changed or corrected.

tips.title: Paraphrase the question
tips.body: In your introduction, do not copy the question. Change the key words and the structure, then state your position.

tips.title: Copy words exactly
tips.body: In gap-fill questions copy the word exactly as it appears in the text, check the word limit, and make sure the answer fits the grammar of the sentence.

tips.title: Extend your answers in Part 1
tips.body: Do not give one-word answers. Say your answer, give a reason, and add a short example: two or three sentences is about right.

tips.title: Answers come in order
tips.body: In every section the answers are heard in the same order as the questions. If you miss one, let it go and listen for the next.

tips.title: Accuracy beats length
tips.body: A few complex sentences that are correct are better than many long sentences full of mistakes. Keep your grammar under control.

tips.title: Always write an overview
tips.body: In Task 1, one or two sentences about the main trends or the biggest differences is the key part of a good answer. Do not give opinions.

lines: These days, many young people choose to start their own business rather than work for a company.
Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Some people believe that it is best to accept a bad situation, such as an unsatisfying job or a shortage of money. Others argue that it is better to try to improve such situations.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
In many cities, the amount of rubbish that people throw away is increasing every year.
What are the causes of this problem? What measures could be taken to reduce the amount of rubbish?
Some people believe that individuals can do very little to slow climate change, and that only governments and large companies can make a real difference.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Many people today prefer to buy goods online rather than in shops.
Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?
International tourism has grown enormously in recent decades, and many places now receive millions of foreign visitors every year.
Is this a positive or negative development for the countries that tourists visit?
In many countries, children and young people are spending less time outdoors than in the past.
Why is this happening? What can be done to encourage them to spend more time outside?
Some people believe that technology has made our lives more complicated. Others think that it has made life much easier.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Some people think that schools should spend more time teaching practical skills, such as cooking and managing money, than academic subjects.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Some people believe that robots and artificial intelligence will create more jobs than they destroy. Others think that they will lead to widespread unemployment.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
In some countries, children begin learning a foreign language at primary school rather than at secondary school.
Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

Some people say that the best way to improve public health is to increase the number of sports facilities. Others, however, believe that this would have little effect and that other measures are required.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Some students take a year off between finishing school and starting university, in order to work or to travel.
Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Some people believe that unpaid community service, such as helping in hospitals or cleaning parks, should be a compulsory part of high school programmes.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Some people think that spending large amounts of money on space exploration is a waste when there are so many problems that need solving on Earth.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Some people believe that newspapers, magazines and websites should not be allowed to report on the private lives of famous people.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Some people believe that homework should be banned for children at primary school.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
In many countries, the number of children who are overweight is increasing.
What are the causes of this problem? What solutions can you suggest?
In many countries, an increasing number of people are choosing to live alone.
What are the reasons for this trend? Do you think it is a positive or negative development?
Noise in cities has become a serious problem, affecting people's health and quality of life.
What are the main causes of noise in cities? What can be done to reduce it?
Some people think that art and music should be compulsory subjects for all students until the age of sixteen.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
In many countries, the gap between the richest and the poorest people is increasing.
What problems does this cause? What solutions can you suggest?
Some people think that governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
In many countries, fewer and fewer young people are choosing to become farmers.
Why is this happening? What can be done to encourage more young people to work in farming?
Some people believe that all advertising aimed at children should be banned.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Increasingly, people are choosing to take courses online instead of attending classes in person.
Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Some people think that children should begin their formal education at a very early age. Others believe that children should not start school until they are at least seven years old.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Some people think that the main purpose of a university education is to give students academic knowledge, while others believe that universities should prepare students for the world of work.
Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
Some people believe that rich countries should give much more financial aid to poorer countries.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Today, many people get their news from social media rather than from newspapers, television or radio.
Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?

In many countries, people are living longer than ever before. Some people believe that an ageing population creates serious problems for governments. Others think that there are benefits if a society has more elderly people.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
More and more people are choosing to work from home rather than travelling to an office every day.
Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
In many cities, museums and historical sites are visited mainly by tourists rather than by local people.
Why is this the case? What can be done to encourage more local people to visit them?
In many parts of the world, traditional languages are dying out because fewer and fewer people speak them.
Why is this happening? Does it matter if some languages disappear?
Some people think that it is better for children to grow up in the countryside. Others believe that cities offer children a better environment.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
